title: Kentucky Coffeetree: Ancient Coffeetrees You Can Visit
meta_description: Named for settlers who roasted its seeds as coffee, toxic raw. Bordeaux's, over 130 years old, is fenced and pruned around cavities in its trunk.
intro: The genus this tree belongs to has exactly two species in the world, this one and a Chinese cousin, and it survives mostly because people kept planting it. The Kentucky coffeetree takes its English name from settlers who roasted and ground its seeds as a coffee substitute, a recipe not worth reviving since the raw seeds and pods are toxic. What gives it away is timing: it leafs out later than almost anything nearby, often not before late May, then drops early and spends the rest of the year as bare, blunt grey branches, so stark that the Dutch call it the dead men's bones tree and the French call it chicot, stump. Bordeaux's, over 130 years old, is fenced and pruned around cavities in its trunk. Ottawa's went in near Queen Elizabeth Driveway around the turn of the twentieth century, and Idaho's largest stands in Boise's Julia Davis Park.
